full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing, we’re looking at women and engineering and what it’s like being in a male dominated industry and women’s first experiences of the industry. We had really planned to interview students that were going on placement before, during and after their placements, but we’ve been having a few problems trying to find some placement students so we decided to include the part time students as well, because they’ve got some experience of the industry. So have you just finished your third year?

Subject:	Third year of the course.

Interviewer:	OK. Is it mechanical engineering you’re doing?

Subject:	Yes, that’s right.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, what ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	English, Maths and Physics.

Interviewer:	OK and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Oh just a comprehensive school.

Interviewer:	Yeah – OK. Before you started on your course did you have any other work experience?

Subject:	Just an Optician’s (?) not engineering related, no.

Interviewer:	Right, that’s fine. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

Subject:	Yeah, my Dad is, he works for the Gas Board – it’s kind of engineering-ish.

Interviewer:	When and why do you think you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Er, it’s funny because when I started my ‘A’ levels, I wanted to be an Optician – that’s what I was going to go for but somewhere along the line I just changed my mind and when I was looking through all the prospectuses, I just decided really – to do it, cos I’ve always been kind of interested in making things and things – like practical things. (Yeah) So I just – yeah, I just decided and so I applied for it and when I applied to University, I applied for a couple of engineering courses, and a maths course and an English course but then I just decided that I wanted to do the engineering (yeah) so it’s just – I dunno really – it just happened (laughs).

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think the fact that your Dad was kind of involved in the industry played any role or..?

Subject:	I think so, yeah. Not directly but I think subconsciously it must have, it definitely made me want to do something like that, so yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you have any careers advice or anything like that, when you were at school?

Subject:	We did, but erm nothing – nothing that helped really (laughs).

Interviewer:	OK, what is it, do you think, that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	I don’t know. I don’t know really – I think it probably is because it’s like (sighs) er like a practical side of things, isn’t it, (yeah) rather than all – so I suppose you can get involved in things like that, I think that’s probably what appeals to me.
Interviewer:	And what about specifically mechanical engineering? Did you ever consider say doing civil engineering or…?

Subject:	No. Mechanical – erm, appealed to me the most straight away, rather than electrics and things like that. Er, I think my Physics ‘A’ level made me realise I didn’t want to do electronics or erm – and civil didn’t appeal to me either. So yeah, I just – I just looked at the range of colleges that appealed to me most.

Interviewer:	OK, and what appealed to you about the network 75 programme?

Subject:	It’s funny, cos’ when I applied to the college, I applied to quite a few different courses here and then the Network 75 was just a leaflet in one of the letters and I hadn’t really read it, and I was just going to throw it and then I had a look and it said about the money and things like that and erm, so that really appealed to me straight away (yeah) because when I was doing my ‘A’ levels, I wrote off to a load of different companies to ask for sponsorship and things like that, so ideally I wanted to work and do a course at the same time (yeah). So when it came through that they’d find you a job and things like that, it was just – it was great. It was just what I wanted, so. Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider going to another University or maybe studying full-time at all or…?

Subject:	I applied to [university] as well and – yeah, if I hadn’t have got a job or the Network 75, I would have done it full time.

Interviewer:	You would have done this course then?

Subject:	Yeah, I just really what – yeah, all the engineering courses I applied for was here – I wanted to come here really. It’s just because I wanted to stay at home (yeah) and so it was either going to be [this university] or [university] and it just – it was - the Network 75 - just made me want to come here.

Interviewer:	OK, when you first decided that you wanted to do engineering, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. I think I – I was under no illusion if you know what I mean – yeah, yeah…

Interviewer:	Were your ‘A’ level courses quite male dominated as well?

Subject:	Yeah, because in Physics there was not many of us – there was only about 2 girls and the rest were boys, so I’m quite used to it really (laughs)

Interviewer:	It didn’t ever concern you at all?

Subject:	No, no.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to go into engineering?

Subject:	I think so, because I find it really interesting and I enjoy it, and then there’s nothing you can’t do because you’re a woman, I think.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Why do you think that more women don’t do it?

Subject:	I think it’s probably because they’re more interested in things like History and English and things like – because my mother, she’s not interested in it at all. She can’t understand like what – I don’t know. There’s more other things, I think, that women would like (Yes). Men like prefer this kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s all to do with how men and women are brought up?

Subject:	I think so yeah, yeah, because I used to like building things like getting a kit and making – so I like to do things like that, rather than play with dolls too much, do you know what I mean? Yeah I think that was – it must influence you somehow, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think could be done then, at say an early stage in education or something, to encourage more women into engineering?

Subject:	I think – maybe you could do, like in school you do a few experiments, don’t you? If you did more – and more interesting things, rather than just, you know, because I remember just turning on a bulb, for the electric, that kind of thing. If they did more interesting things they’d need – yeah, because most of the subjects in school, like English and History and Geography – the basic ones and then when you do Technology – you only get, it’s not a large proportion of the week, is it? I think if you did more, focussed more on things like that, it might lead more people into.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you feel make a good engineer?

Subject:	 (laughs) Erm, you have to be like a team work. I think you have to be able to follow things through logically. You have to be able to analyse problems and stuff like that. Erm, yeah, you mustn’t just go in thinking your opinion’s right and it’s gonna work how you – so you have to look at all the different aspects and then think oh that’s alright, that’s the right way. I dunno really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things are what people would think are more male characteristics and more female characteristics?

Subject:	I don’t know. (laughs) Er, …

Interviewer:	Not necessarily that they are, but what people perceive?

Subject:	I think if people thought of engineering, they’d think you have to be like big and strong (yeah) and so they think of men, I think, straight away. Yeah, I – it’s just you think of engineering and you think of men and you think of like garages and things like that, don’t you? So erm, I think yeah, people would think the traits are male but yeah …

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Er, it’s good. Erm, it depends on you. It’s not – I found it good because I’ve always had more boy friends than girl friends, and so I’m just used to it and it’s not an issue for me or anything but I think you could feel a bit awkward because you are singled out because you’re the girl, but it doesn’t really bother me too much. But if you were a bit insecure I think that could really affect you because in every lesson it’s like guys and lady – they make a point of it – only trying to be nice (yeah) but that could affect it.

Interviewer:	OK, and are you the only girl on your course?

Subject:	Yeah. There’s a few classes where we meet up with other – with other subjects and so we’ve got 4 girls then, so generally yeah, I’m the only girl.

Interviewer:	OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Mostly. I think yeah – because I’m doing a BEng, I knew it wouldn’t be as practical as the BSc’s or something like that, but most of the subjects have been fine. There’s a few, which are just new I suppose, different to what you’ve done at school and things like but yeah, it mostly is – it’s mostly been …

Interviewer:	Was there any particular reason that you wanted to do the BEng rather than the BSc?

Subject:	Not really. I didn’t realise the difference until I started, but I had the points to go in, so I thought I may as well do the best I can (yeah) kind of thing, yeah. I didn’t realise I’d probably just didn’t know you could do the BSc and Network 75, I thought you had to do the BEng and so – but yeah, I’m glad I’m doing them now, because I think some of the modules seem a bit more interesting – yeah.

Interviewer:	Is the BEng course accredited?

Subject:	I don’t think so. I’m not sure though.

Interviewer:	That’s fine – what would you say have been the best and the worse things about the course, so far?

Subject:	I think – mm, the best thing I’ve had loads of experiences, like I’m being interviewed by you now (yeah) and I’ve been in the paper and things like that – yes, so that’s quite – they’re probably the best things, yeah, because I’m a girl and engineer I get a lot of opportunities and things like that – that’s good. The worst thing though was this year we had all our assignments – they were all between Christmas and Easter and so it was horrible. We had loads and loads on, so that was, I think, probably the worst time trying to – because you’re still going to work in the day (yeah) and then you’ve got to come home and do your homework on the weekends – I think that’s the hardest bit.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	One – in the first year we had a drawing lesson and she was a female one, but I think we only had her for like half the year as well, so that’s the only time. (Really?) Yeah.

Interviewer:	Alright – do you think you’d find that encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	I don’t know really – probably. Erm, as long as they were good it wouldn’t matter, what they are – you know, whether they’re male or female. It probably would be a bit nicer though sometimes because you can chat a bit more.(laughs)

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat male and female students the same? You’ve said that you sort of get singled out sometimes.

Subject:	Yeah, I think so – I’ve never felt otherwise, but I know some people have said that they think – cos where I work there’s another girl on the course, and she said she’s had some of her lecturers, she thinks have been a bit sexist but erm, to me personally, I haven’t had that. I don’t mind if they say lady – cos’ they say ‘lady and gents’, I think it’s quite funny, it doesn’t bother me because if they just said ‘gents’ or whatever it wouldn’t bother me, but er no, I’ve never felt awkward about it really. Erm, one of our lecturers – I mean he just makes like women jokes, which are alright, they’re not offensive, but it – you just get bored with them, every lesson, do you know what I mean? But erm yeah, no, most of them are really fine.

Interviewer:	OK, do you have a personal tutor?

Subject:	No. Do you mean in the college? (Yeah) No, not that I know of.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know – what do you mean? What do you mean?

Interviewer:	Well, like a lecturer that’s been really sort of…

Subject:	Encouraging…

Interviewer:	Encouraging or motivated you. Or friends that have motivated you, or someone at work, or – there might not have been…

Subject:	No, I don’t think so really. No, nobody in particular. I think because I’m on the Network 75 scheme, I feel more motivated, like I have to work harder because – because of the consequences – do you know what I mean? I want to keep on working, so I have to work hard. So I think that has influenced – but nothing in particular.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had to do much group work as part of the course?

Subject:	A little bit. Erm, yeah, this year they had two projects, group work – but not much at all, only the odd one.

Interviewer:	Right, do you like doing group work?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Why not?

Subject:	It depends who you’re working with. If you’re working with a group you like and they’re all working hard as well, that’s great, but I don’t like it because you can’t make them all work and they don’t all work as hard as you’d like, and so, sometimes you feel a bit let down by them and you know, if you’d done it on your own you could have got a better mark. I don’t like that side of it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, because they leave me to do all the organising. Erm, yeah, we’ll all sit down and discuss it and you know, what do you want kind of thing, but I’ll take – I don’t know whether that’s just me, or if it’s because I’m quite organised, so I’ll take the lead and I’ll say look, we’ll all do this and so yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you had any particularly bad experiences with group work?

Subject:	Yeah (laughs)

Interviewer:	What happened?

Subject:	Er, this year – we had one really good group work that – with the Network 75, there’s 5 of us in our class, and there’s 3 of us work together brilliantly (yeah) and we had a good mark and I think we felt a bit obliged to have the other 2 in as well, because we’d like left them out a bit, so we did an (?) and they’d turn up late and they couldn’t be bothered and so we had a bad mark – yeah. We had like 42% something really bad! And we’d all done good work but they just hadn’t bothered at all and so…

Interviewer:	Yeah, it’s just lets the whole side down…

Subject:	Yeah, that disappointed me, because in that assignment – in some of the group ones you have to write like an introduction of things that you’ve contributed to it (right) but we didn’t have any of that in this assignment, it was just – so they didn’t know who had done what kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that doing group work at Uni is a good experience for doing group stuff or just being in a working environment?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so, yeah, because where I work is in – we are in teams, so you have to get on with everybody else. Yeah, I think it does teach you to like appreciate other people’s opinions and their ideas and things. Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you use the skills that you’re learning in classroom at work?

Subject:	No, not really (laughs). None of them directly apply. Erm, I think by doing what you do in Uni – you appreciate what’s going on in work, but nothing links directly at all, no.

Interviewer:	OK. What about the opposite way round – do you use the things you’ve learnt at work, or do the things that you’ve learnt at work help you put into perspective what you’ve been doing at Uni?

Subject:	None of the practical things. I think just the fact that you’ve got – you’ve got deadlines and things in work, it helps you with the Uni side of it, I think. (Yeah) Just being organised and things like that – you have to be at work and so I think I’ve brought that into the Uni side of it, but erm, yeah, that’s it really.

Interviewer:	OK. Can you tell me a bit about the company that you’re working for? Like what they do, how big they are and…

Subject:	Yeah. It’s called [name] and we do like aircraft engines – we kind of like manage the maintenance of that. So we don’t do physical things and it’s office based, but they go out and do inspections of all the different like airfields and things like that and it’s quite small but it’s growing. When I started it was a lot smaller than it is now. There’s about 40 people now and it’s getting bigger all the time. You’re kind of – you have like a contract with a fleet, so they’ll look after the engines and decide when they need to be taken (off ring?) and fixed and things like that, and they’ll just do all – all like the jobs. The airlines can just say oh, you know, tell us when it needs to be done – tell us the dates and we’ll do all the other side of it and check the invoices and things like that, and yeah, and just keep them up to date and all because these documents come out all the time, which means you have to change something in the engine or you have to update it – things like this. So we just keep track of all of those. So we do kind of like a long-term fleet thing, we’ll have them for like 3 years and we’ll sort it all out for them. They also do like one-off consultancy projects and things like that, and just inspections in places, just like one-off things or whatever. So, yeah, it is interesting – it’s quite different, considering there’s only a small amount of people, they do – they go to a lot of different places all around the world (yeah) and we’ve signed some big contracts lately, with like large (?) companies and so that’s increased the portfolio even more, and it’s – yeah, it’s really good.

Interviewer:	Are there many women working in the company?

Subject:	No, there’s erm, there’s 4 I think – 1,2,3…- 5 altogether (yeah) 2 of us in engineering, 1 of them is in like the finance side of it and then another aspect of it is they buy and sell parts for engines and 2 of them are in there, so, yeah, it’s not many.

Interviewer:	Did you have a choice of which company you could go and work for?

Subject:	No. No, what they did – I signed, I filled in an application form to go on network 75, and then they just sent me a letter then saying I’ve got an interview with [company], where I work now. And then – so I went to the interview and I got it, so I accepted that because I liked it. I know other people had a couple of different interviews in other places and I think because I liked it straight away and they accepted, that didn’t matter to me.

Interviewer:	Yeah – you just thought you’d go for it. (Yeah) OK, you’ve probably touched a bit on this already, but do you think there are any advantages or disadvantages to studying part-time and doing the network 75 then?

Subject:	Erm, the major advantage is you get paid (yeah) and you’re doing work that does kind of relate really, do you know – not directly but it’s engineering isn’t it, so it goes well, otherwise I’d have to work in a shop or a pub or something like that. So I’d rather do it – do it linked to it. Erm, yeah I like that – it’s like stability I suppose, isn’t it, a bit? I don’t like it when you’ve got lots of homework on and things like that. I find it really hard then cos after a day’s work you’re tired and you can’t be bothered to do anything. To motivate yourself then is really hard – so I don’t like that side of it.

Interviewer:	How does – how long is your course with doing it part-time, is it five years?

Subject:	Five years – yeah.

Interviewer:	So you’re doing more than – you must be doing more than a full year. If you were doing a full-time course (yeah) that’d be 3 years.

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, a lot of extra work. Yeah – if you did a – what I was planning to do, if I did a full-time would be to do a year out as well. So I used to justify to myself – say there’s only 4 years, so it’s only a year extra. So yeah – yeah you do have to work, in work all over the summer holidays and all the other days, because it works out we do 3 days in work and then 2 days in college. So, yeah, say there’s 10 modules in a year, in University we do 8 or 7, or something like that. So that’s how it splits out.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the best and the worst things about being on the placement?

Subject:	Hmm – ooh, the best is the experience you get because you get to know working life, what that’s all about and then, yeah, you get involved in different things and so I think that’s probably the best aspect of it, just – you are actually doing proper work (yeah) and it’s long-term it’s what you want to be doing as well. And the disadvantages – oh, I think because you come in as a new person and you’re not there all the time, that – they find that quite hard to give you like big projects or things like that because yeah, I think that’s quite an issue, from the work perspective. Because you’re only there a few days a week, they think oh we can’t give them that to do because that needs to be done yeah – so I think that’s probably the worse aspect of it, it’s sometimes you miss out on things because you’re not there.

Interviewer:	Yeah, yeah – I’ve not thought about that actually, that’s quite interesting. Are there any other students at the company?

Subject:	No, but they are taking one on for next year.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. How do you think that being at work differs from being at University – how you’re treated, and what’s expected of you and things like that?

Subject:	Yeah. In Uni, you’re more left – I know you’ve got to turn up, but you’re left to your own devices how you do the work and when you do it. But in work you’ve got to do it (yeah) – it’s more, it’s more strict, more disciplined I suppose. Erm, yeah, in a way it’s more monotonous, because in Uni, you have a lect… – you might have a break in between and you – you’re going to all different places and things like that, but in work once you’re in, you’re there for the day and then – yeah, even though in Uni I end up working later, because some of the lectures don’t finish till after – say half six, things like that, yet tends to go quicker than if you finish at 5 in work. And er…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the course and the placement might fit together quite well, or do you see them as like two totally separate things really?

Subject:	It – it depends really. I think overall they work well but it is hard to get your head round, I think. The first year was quite hard to get used to Uni and to get used to work and yeah – but once – like the second year come along it was fine, you’re into the routine of it, you know what’s expected of you from both sides and yeah I think it goes well. The worst thing is just when you’ve got a lot of homework when you wish you had a day off.

Interviewer:	Yeah – do you think you’ve encountered any issues at work that you think are a result of being a woman?

Subject:	Not so much of - oh yeah, a really petty thing, erm every so often they used to do like a breakfast meeting and they’d have like croissants and bagels and things like that, and if – if the people who don’t do it are away, instead of just asking anybody would you like to do it? They ask me, because, or another girl – it’s never – cos it’s all men, who are all willing to do it, who all eat the breakfast as well (yeah) and it’s yeah, the fact that oh because you’re a girl, obviously you can cook. It’s only like for (??) things like that. So yeah, that’s the worst thing – so that’s the only – I think that’s the only time I’ve felt it and it’s only – it’s petty because it’s not even related to the work – so yeah, it’s like – I wouldn’t mind doing it, if they’d asked everybody, I think I’d volunteer, but just – because they like asked for you, I don’t like it. (laughs)

Interviewer:	Do you say anything to them or just keep quiet?

Subject:	Er, no, I just keep quiet really. Yeah, I think people know what I think about it really (laughs).

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased you decided to do the Network 75?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely – yeah, overall I really enjoy it, even though there’s like hard bits and yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think it might improve your career prospects at the end?

Subject:	I think so, because you’ve got a degree and you’ve got 5 years experience already before you’ve even done anything really. So yeah I do think so. And I think because I’ve had to do – deal with lots of different things, just throughout mixing them both together, I think it’s put me in a good standing for a job.

Interviewer:	Yeah, definitely. OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	No idea (laughs). Erm, I keep changing…

Interviewer:	Will you be an Engineer?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I would still but sometimes I think I’ll stay where I am. Sometimes I think I could do teaching or something like that (yeah) and then, I’ve no idea really (laughs).

Interviewer:	Would you stay with the company, if they offered you a job?

Subject:	I would, yeah, yeah. I dunno if like forever, but I think initially, I definitely would, yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok. What would be your ideal career then, do you think?

Subject:	Erm, probably working 3 days a week. I would like that. Erm, yeah, because you’re used to being – you’re used to the weeks being split up. When you have to do the summer, it’s 5 days a week and it’s really boring.

Interviewer:	It is quite interesting what you said about it being part-time as well, because some of the people that I’ve interviewed – students at [name] University as well, that are going on the placement and some of them have talked about more long-term, if they decided to have a family what happens (oh yeah?) and stuff like that, and especially people in construction side of things, because it’s a lot of site work and that, they’re saying you can’t really work part-time (that’s true) stuff like that, so I don’t know what we’d do if we had kids and things like that (yeah) whether we’d probably have to go into consultancy rather than site work, so it is interesting that they are actually – even though it is quite difficult for them, they are doing it.

Subject:	Yeah – no, I do think that. I wouldn’t like to work full time if I had a family – I wouldn’t like that at all. But erm – yeah – or even if – just after I got married or whatever, I’d quite like to work 3 days a week (laughs)

Interviewer:	I’d quite like that too.

Subject:	I don’t know if I could get away with it really, that’s why I think teaching because you get a whole summer off don’t you? So yeah, yeah, even though I like – I do enjoy work but I’m not like a career, career person. If I had a family and things I would stop but I wouldn’t – I’d work, I wouldn’t have to think oh I have to be a Manager or what ever, as long as I’m doing something I enjoy, it wouldn’t matter too much really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are quite good in mechanical engineering?

Subject:	I think so, because there’s such a broad range of things you could do, like at the moment its aeroplane engines, there’s loads and loads of different things you could do yeah. And then, like lecturing, and things like that you could do as well, so I think – and if you were willing to move, not necessarily abroad, but definitely around Wales – England as well, I think, yeah, I think there’s a lot of different opportunities really.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like to stay local to here or…?

Subject:	I’m a – I don’t mind either really. I’m not opposed to moving. I think really – realistically I realise that I probably have to move away, because it’s not – there a lot of places in [town], but it’s not like loads. There’s probably more opportunities elsewhere (yeah) so I don’t know really. Probably, I’d probably like to go away say for 10 years or something like that, but I maybe move back eventually, something like that I think.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	No, I think I’d probably do it the same – yeah. I think I’d probably stick with this.

Interviewer:	That’s good. What 5 words would you use to describe the engineering industry?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. That’s really hard that is, isn’t it? (Yeah) Varied I think, there’s lot of different – challenging. It is male, so I probably would say male because yeah, we’re way out numbered.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that it’s masculine is to do with the numbers of men, or is it the type of work as well?

Subject:	I think it’s probably the type – yeah, and yeah, I think yeah, it’s probably a mixture of both really than any other type of work – because in that, even though in our company there’s only a few girls, and all the other people you have dealings with they’re all men as well, there’s hardly any – you notice the odd woman. Erm, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you ever think that the fact that it is so masculine will cause you any problems at all or…?

Subject:	I think it could. I think it just depends on people and how they react to it because erm, yeah, like it doesn’t bother me, it could bother some women. It could also bother some men I think. They might think oh it’s like a boys’ club kind of thing and then there’s a girl in the way, so I wonder if they would think. I think they would act differently if there was no women about, definitely. Erm, yes, I think…

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will improve for women in the industry?

Subject:	I’ve never really thought about it. I think it probably will because erm as women are becoming more independent and things like that, and they’re making their career choices, rather than just jobs, things like that, so I think eventually they will look into it – more will look into engineering and so it would improve that way. But I think the industry could appeal more to women if it – somehow – it could do something to make it more appealing, because it’s not all – like I work in an office, so it’s not – you’re not covered in oil or anything like that. It’s just like office work, with a different application really, so that – that’s absolutely fine for women (yeah) – so I think yeah, I think eventually it’ll probably become more female as well. I think it’ll always be male (yeah) but there might be more women.

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK that’s everything you’ve been very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing, we’re looking at women and engineering and what it’s like being in a male dominated industry and women’s first experiences of the industry. We had really planned to interview students that were going on placement before, during and after their placements, but we’ve been having a few problems trying to find some placement students so we decided to include the part time students as well, because they’ve got some experience of the industry. So have you just finished your third year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Third year of the course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Is it mechanical engineering you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, that’s right.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do ‘A’ levels?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: English, Maths and Physics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh just a comprehensive school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – OK. Before you started on your course did you have any other work experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just an Optician’s (?) not engineering related, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, that’s fine. Are either of your parents engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, my Dad is, he works for the Gas Board – it’s kind of engineering-ish.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When and why do you think you decided to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it’s funny because when I started my ‘A’ levels, I wanted to be an Optician – that’s what I was going to go for but somewhere along the line I just changed my mind and when I was looking through all the prospectuses, I just decided really – to do it, cos I’ve always been kind of interested in making things and things – like practical things. (Yeah) So I just – yeah, I just decided and so I applied for it and when I applied to University, I applied for a couple of engineering courses, and a maths course and an English course but then I just decided that I wanted to do the engineering (yeah) so it’s just – I dunno really – it just happened (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think the fact that your Dad was kind of involved in the industry played any role or..?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yeah. Not directly but I think subconsciously it must have, it definitely made me want to do something like that, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have any careers advice or anything like that, when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We did, but erm nothing – nothing that helped really (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what is it, do you think, that appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I don’t know really – I think it probably is because it’s like (sighs) er like a practical side of things, isn’t it, (yeah) rather than all – so I suppose you can get involved in things like that, I think that’s probably what appeals to me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what about specifically mechanical engineering? Did you ever consider say doing civil engineering or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Mechanical – erm, appealed to me the most straight away, rather than electrics and things like that. Er, I think my Physics ‘A’ level made me realise I didn’t want to do electronics or erm – and civil didn’t appeal to me either. So yeah, I just – I just looked at the range of colleges that appealed to me most.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what appealed to you about the network 75 programme?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s funny, cos’ when I applied to the college, I applied to quite a few different courses here and then the Network 75 was just a leaflet in one of the letters and I hadn’t really read it, and I was just going to throw it and then I had a look and it said about the money and things like that and erm, so that really appealed to me straight away (yeah) because when I was doing my ‘A’ levels, I wrote off to a load of different companies to ask for sponsorship and things like that, so ideally I wanted to work and do a course at the same time (yeah). So when it came through that they’d find you a job and things like that, it was just – it was great. It was just what I wanted, so. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider going to another University or maybe studying full-time at all or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I applied to [university] as well and – yeah, if I hadn’t have got a job or the Network 75, I would have done it full time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You would have done this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I just really what – yeah, all the engineering courses I applied for was here – I wanted to come here really. It’s just because I wanted to stay at home (yeah) and so it was either going to be [this university] or [university] and it just – it was - the Network 75 - just made me want to come here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you first decided that you wanted to do engineering, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. I think I – I was under no illusion if you know what I mean – yeah, yeah…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were your ‘A’ level courses quite male dominated as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because in Physics there was not many of us – there was only about 2 girls and the rest were boys, so I’m quite used to it really (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It didn’t ever concern you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to go into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, because I find it really interesting and I enjoy it, and then there’s nothing you can’t do because you’re a woman, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Why do you think that more women don’t do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s probably because they’re more interested in things like History and English and things like – because my mother, she’s not interested in it at all. She can’t understand like what – I don’t know. There’s more other things, I think, that women would like (Yes). Men like prefer this kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s all to do with how men and women are brought up?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yeah, yeah, because I used to like building things like getting a kit and making – so I like to do things like that, rather than play with dolls too much, do you know what I mean? Yeah I think that was – it must influence you somehow, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think could be done then, at say an early stage in education or something, to encourage more women into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – maybe you could do, like in school you do a few experiments, don’t you? If you did more – and more interesting things, rather than just, you know, because I remember just turning on a bulb, for the electric, that kind of thing. If they did more interesting things they’d need – yeah, because most of the subjects in school, like English and History and Geography – the basic ones and then when you do Technology – you only get, it’s not a large proportion of the week, is it? I think if you did more, focussed more on things like that, it might lead more people into.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you feel make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (laughs) Erm, you have to be like a team work. I think you have to be able to follow things through logically. You have to be able to analyse problems and stuff like that. Erm, yeah, you mustn’t just go in thinking your opinion’s right and it’s gonna work how you – so you have to look at all the different aspects and then think oh that’s alright, that’s the right way. I dunno really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things are what people would think are more male characteristics and more female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. (laughs) Er, …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not necessarily that they are, but what people perceive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think if people thought of engineering, they’d think you have to be like big and strong (yeah) and so they think of men, I think, straight away. Yeah, I – it’s just you think of engineering and you think of men and you think of like garages and things like that, don’t you? So erm, I think yeah, people would think the traits are male but yeah …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it’s good. Erm, it depends on you. It’s not – I found it good because I’ve always had more boy friends than girl friends, and so I’m just used to it and it’s not an issue for me or anything but I think you could feel a bit awkward because you are singled out because you’re the girl, but it doesn’t really bother me too much. But if you were a bit insecure I think that could really affect you because in every lesson it’s like guys and lady – they make a point of it – only trying to be nice (yeah) but that could affect it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and are you the only girl on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. There’s a few classes where we meet up with other – with other subjects and so we’ve got 4 girls then, so generally yeah, I’m the only girl.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mostly. I think yeah – because I’m doing a BEng, I knew it wouldn’t be as practical as the BSc’s or something like that, but most of the subjects have been fine. There’s a few, which are just new I suppose, different to what you’ve done at school and things like but yeah, it mostly is – it’s mostly been …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was there any particular reason that you wanted to do the BEng rather than the BSc?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I didn’t realise the difference until I started, but I had the points to go in, so I thought I may as well do the best I can (yeah) kind of thing, yeah. I didn’t realise I’d probably just didn’t know you could do the BSc and Network 75, I thought you had to do the BEng and so – but yeah, I’m glad I’m doing them now, because I think some of the modules seem a bit more interesting – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is the BEng course accredited?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so. I’m not sure though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s fine – what would you say have been the best and the worse things about the course, so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – mm, the best thing I’ve had loads of experiences, like I’m being interviewed by you now (yeah) and I’ve been in the paper and things like that – yes, so that’s quite – they’re probably the best things, yeah, because I’m a girl and engineer I get a lot of opportunities and things like that – that’s good. The worst thing though was this year we had all our assignments – they were all between Christmas and Easter and so it was horrible. We had loads and loads on, so that was, I think, probably the worst time trying to – because you’re still going to work in the day (yeah) and then you’ve got to come home and do your homework on the weekends – I think that’s the hardest bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One – in the first year we had a drawing lesson and she was a female one, but I think we only had her for like half the year as well, so that’s the only time. (Really?) Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Alright – do you think you’d find that encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know really – probably. Erm, as long as they were good it wouldn’t matter, what they are – you know, whether they’re male or female. It probably would be a bit nicer though sometimes because you can chat a bit more.(laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the lecturers treat male and female students the same? You’ve said that you sort of get singled out sometimes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so – I’ve never felt otherwise, but I know some people have said that they think – cos where I work there’s another girl on the course, and she said she’s had some of her lecturers, she thinks have been a bit sexist but erm, to me personally, I haven’t had that. I don’t mind if they say lady – cos’ they say ‘lady and gents’, I think it’s quite funny, it doesn’t bother me because if they just said ‘gents’ or whatever it wouldn’t bother me, but er no, I’ve never felt awkward about it really. Erm, one of our lecturers – I mean he just makes like women jokes, which are alright, they’re not offensive, but it – you just get bored with them, every lesson, do you know what I mean? But erm yeah, no, most of them are really fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you have a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Do you mean in the college? (Yeah) No, not that I know of.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know – what do you mean? What do you mean?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well, like a lecturer that’s been really sort of…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Encouraging…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Encouraging or motivated you. Or friends that have motivated you, or someone at work, or – there might not have been…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think so really. No, nobody in particular. I think because I’m on the Network 75 scheme, I feel more motivated, like I have to work harder because – because of the consequences – do you know what I mean? I want to keep on working, so I have to work hard. So I think that has influenced – but nothing in particular.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had to do much group work as part of the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A little bit. Erm, yeah, this year they had two projects, group work – but not much at all, only the odd one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It depends who you’re working with. If you’re working with a group you like and they’re all working hard as well, that’s great, but I don’t like it because you can’t make them all work and they don’t all work as hard as you’d like, and so, sometimes you feel a bit let down by them and you know, if you’d done it on your own you could have got a better mark. I don’t like that side of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, because they leave me to do all the organising. Erm, yeah, we’ll all sit down and discuss it and you know, what do you want kind of thing, but I’ll take – I don’t know whether that’s just me, or if it’s because I’m quite organised, so I’ll take the lead and I’ll say look, we’ll all do this and so yeah, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you had any particularly bad experiences with group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, this year – we had one really good group work that – with the Network 75, there’s 5 of us in our class, and there’s 3 of us work together brilliantly (yeah) and we had a good mark and I think we felt a bit obliged to have the other 2 in as well, because we’d like left them out a bit, so we did an (?) and they’d turn up late and they couldn’t be bothered and so we had a bad mark – yeah. We had like 42% something really bad! And we’d all done good work but they just hadn’t bothered at all and so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, it’s just lets the whole side down…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, that disappointed me, because in that assignment – in some of the group ones you have to write like an introduction of things that you’ve contributed to it (right) but we didn’t have any of that in this assignment, it was just – so they didn’t know who had done what kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing group work at Uni is a good experience for doing group stuff or just being in a working environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so, yeah, because where I work is in – we are in teams, so you have to get on with everybody else. Yeah, I think it does teach you to like appreciate other people’s opinions and their ideas and things. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you use the skills that you’re learning in classroom at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really (laughs). None of them directly apply. Erm, I think by doing what you do in Uni – you appreciate what’s going on in work, but nothing links directly at all, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What about the opposite way round – do you use the things you’ve learnt at work, or do the things that you’ve learnt at work help you put into perspective what you’ve been doing at Uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: None of the practical things. I think just the fact that you’ve got – you’ve got deadlines and things in work, it helps you with the Uni side of it, I think. (Yeah) Just being organised and things like that – you have to be at work and so I think I’ve brought that into the Uni side of it, but erm, yeah, that’s it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Can you tell me a bit about the company that you’re working for? Like what they do, how big they are and…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It’s called [name] and we do like aircraft engines – we kind of like manage the maintenance of that. So we don’t do physical things and it’s office based, but they go out and do inspections of all the different like airfields and things like that and it’s quite small but it’s growing. When I started it was a lot smaller than it is now. There’s about 40 people now and it’s getting bigger all the time. You’re kind of – you have like a contract with a fleet, so they’ll look after the engines and decide when they need to be taken (off ring?) and fixed and things like that, and they’ll just do all – all like the jobs. The airlines can just say oh, you know, tell us when it needs to be done – tell us the dates and we’ll do all the other side of it and check the invoices and things like that, and yeah, and just keep them up to date and all because these documents come out all the time, which means you have to change something in the engine or you have to update it – things like this. So we just keep track of all of those. So we do kind of like a long-term fleet thing, we’ll have them for like 3 years and we’ll sort it all out for them. They also do like one-off consultancy projects and things like that, and just inspections in places, just like one-off things or whatever. So, yeah, it is interesting – it’s quite different, considering there’s only a small amount of people, they do – they go to a lot of different places all around the world (yeah) and we’ve signed some big contracts lately, with like large (?) companies and so that’s increased the portfolio even more, and it’s – yeah, it’s really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there many women working in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, there’s erm, there’s 4 I think – 1,2,3…- 5 altogether (yeah) 2 of us in engineering, 1 of them is in like the finance side of it and then another aspect of it is they buy and sell parts for engines and 2 of them are in there, so, yeah, it’s not many.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have a choice of which company you could go and work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No, what they did – I signed, I filled in an application form to go on network 75, and then they just sent me a letter then saying I’ve got an interview with [company], where I work now. And then – so I went to the interview and I got it, so I accepted that because I liked it. I know other people had a couple of different interviews in other places and I think because I liked it straight away and they accepted, that didn’t matter to me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – you just thought you’d go for it. (Yeah) OK, you’ve probably touched a bit on this already, but do you think there are any advantages or disadvantages to studying part-time and doing the network 75 then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the major advantage is you get paid (yeah) and you’re doing work that does kind of relate really, do you know – not directly but it’s engineering isn’t it, so it goes well, otherwise I’d have to work in a shop or a pub or something like that. So I’d rather do it – do it linked to it. Erm, yeah I like that – it’s like stability I suppose, isn’t it, a bit? I don’t like it when you’ve got lots of homework on and things like that. I find it really hard then cos after a day’s work you’re tired and you can’t be bothered to do anything. To motivate yourself then is really hard – so I don’t like that side of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How does – how long is your course with doing it part-time, is it five years?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Five years – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re doing more than – you must be doing more than a full year. If you were doing a full-time course (yeah) that’d be 3 years.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, a lot of extra work. Yeah – if you did a – what I was planning to do, if I did a full-time would be to do a year out as well. So I used to justify to myself – say there’s only 4 years, so it’s only a year extra. So yeah – yeah you do have to work, in work all over the summer holidays and all the other days, because it works out we do 3 days in work and then 2 days in college. So, yeah, say there’s 10 modules in a year, in University we do 8 or 7, or something like that. So that’s how it splits out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think are the best and the worst things about being on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm – ooh, the best is the experience you get because you get to know working life, what that’s all about and then, yeah, you get involved in different things and so I think that’s probably the best aspect of it, just – you are actually doing proper work (yeah) and it’s long-term it’s what you want to be doing as well. And the disadvantages – oh, I think because you come in as a new person and you’re not there all the time, that – they find that quite hard to give you like big projects or things like that because yeah, I think that’s quite an issue, from the work perspective. Because you’re only there a few days a week, they think oh we can’t give them that to do because that needs to be done yeah – so I think that’s probably the worse aspect of it, it’s sometimes you miss out on things because you’re not there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, yeah – I’ve not thought about that actually, that’s quite interesting. Are there any other students at the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, but they are taking one on for next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK. How do you think that being at work differs from being at University – how you’re treated, and what’s expected of you and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. In Uni, you’re more left – I know you’ve got to turn up, but you’re left to your own devices how you do the work and when you do it. But in work you’ve got to do it (yeah) – it’s more, it’s more strict, more disciplined I suppose. Erm, yeah, in a way it’s more monotonous, because in Uni, you have a lect… – you might have a break in between and you – you’re going to all different places and things like that, but in work once you’re in, you’re there for the day and then – yeah, even though in Uni I end up working later, because some of the lectures don’t finish till after – say half six, things like that, yet tends to go quicker than if you finish at 5 in work. And er…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the course and the placement might fit together quite well, or do you see them as like two totally separate things really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It – it depends really. I think overall they work well but it is hard to get your head round, I think. The first year was quite hard to get used to Uni and to get used to work and yeah – but once – like the second year come along it was fine, you’re into the routine of it, you know what’s expected of you from both sides and yeah I think it goes well. The worst thing is just when you’ve got a lot of homework when you wish you had a day off.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – do you think you’ve encountered any issues at work that you think are a result of being a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not so much of - oh yeah, a really petty thing, erm every so often they used to do like a breakfast meeting and they’d have like croissants and bagels and things like that, and if – if the people who don’t do it are away, instead of just asking anybody would you like to do it? They ask me, because, or another girl – it’s never – cos it’s all men, who are all willing to do it, who all eat the breakfast as well (yeah) and it’s yeah, the fact that oh because you’re a girl, obviously you can cook. It’s only like for (??) things like that. So yeah, that’s the worst thing – so that’s the only – I think that’s the only time I’ve felt it and it’s only – it’s petty because it’s not even related to the work – so yeah, it’s like – I wouldn’t mind doing it, if they’d asked everybody, I think I’d volunteer, but just – because they like asked for you, I don’t like it. (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you say anything to them or just keep quiet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no, I just keep quiet really. Yeah, I think people know what I think about it really (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you pleased you decided to do the Network 75?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely – yeah, overall I really enjoy it, even though there’s like hard bits and yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it might improve your career prospects at the end?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, because you’ve got a degree and you’ve got 5 years experience already before you’ve even done anything really. So yeah I do think so. And I think because I’ve had to do – deal with lots of different things, just throughout mixing them both together, I think it’s put me in a good standing for a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No idea (laughs). Erm, I keep changing…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Will you be an Engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I would still but sometimes I think I’ll stay where I am. Sometimes I think I could do teaching or something like that (yeah) and then, I’ve no idea really (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you stay with the company, if they offered you a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would, yeah, yeah. I dunno if like forever, but I think initially, I definitely would, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. What would be your ideal career then, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, probably working 3 days a week. I would like that. Erm, yeah, because you’re used to being – you’re used to the weeks being split up. When you have to do the summer, it’s 5 days a week and it’s really boring.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It is quite interesting what you said about it being part-time as well, because some of the people that I’ve interviewed – students at [name] University as well, that are going on the placement and some of them have talked about more long-term, if they decided to have a family what happens (oh yeah?) and stuff like that, and especially people in construction side of things, because it’s a lot of site work and that, they’re saying you can’t really work part-time (that’s true) stuff like that, so I don’t know what we’d do if we had kids and things like that (yeah) whether we’d probably have to go into consultancy rather than site work, so it is interesting that they are actually – even though it is quite difficult for them, they are doing it.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – no, I do think that. I wouldn’t like to work full time if I had a family – I wouldn’t like that at all. But erm – yeah – or even if – just after I got married or whatever, I’d quite like to work 3 days a week (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’d quite like that too.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know if I could get away with it really, that’s why I think teaching because you get a whole summer off don’t you? So yeah, yeah, even though I like – I do enjoy work but I’m not like a career, career person. If I had a family and things I would stop but I wouldn’t – I’d work, I wouldn’t have to think oh I have to be a Manager or what ever, as long as I’m doing something I enjoy, it wouldn’t matter too much really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are quite good in mechanical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, because there’s such a broad range of things you could do, like at the moment its aeroplane engines, there’s loads and loads of different things you could do yeah. And then, like lecturing, and things like that you could do as well, so I think – and if you were willing to move, not necessarily abroad, but definitely around Wales – England as well, I think, yeah, I think there’s a lot of different opportunities really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like to stay local to here or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m a – I don’t mind either really. I’m not opposed to moving. I think really – realistically I realise that I probably have to move away, because it’s not – there a lot of places in [town], but it’s not like loads. There’s probably more opportunities elsewhere (yeah) so I don’t know really. Probably, I’d probably like to go away say for 10 years or something like that, but I maybe move back eventually, something like that I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think I’d probably do it the same – yeah. I think I’d probably stick with this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good. What 5 words would you use to describe the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. That’s really hard that is, isn’t it? (Yeah) Varied I think, there’s lot of different – challenging. It is male, so I probably would say male because yeah, we’re way out numbered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that it’s masculine is to do with the numbers of men, or is it the type of work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s probably the type – yeah, and yeah, I think yeah, it’s probably a mixture of both really than any other type of work – because in that, even though in our company there’s only a few girls, and all the other people you have dealings with they’re all men as well, there’s hardly any – you notice the odd woman. Erm, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you ever think that the fact that it is so masculine will cause you any problems at all or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it could. I think it just depends on people and how they react to it because erm, yeah, like it doesn’t bother me, it could bother some women. It could also bother some men I think. They might think oh it’s like a boys’ club kind of thing and then there’s a girl in the way, so I wonder if they would think. I think they would act differently if there was no women about, definitely. Erm, yes, I think…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will improve for women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve never really thought about it. I think it probably will because erm as women are becoming more independent and things like that, and they’re making their career choices, rather than just jobs, things like that, so I think eventually they will look into it – more will look into engineering and so it would improve that way. But I think the industry could appeal more to women if it – somehow – it could do something to make it more appealing, because it’s not all – like I work in an office, so it’s not – you’re not covered in oil or anything like that. It’s just like office work, with a different application really, so that – that’s absolutely fine for women (yeah) – so I think yeah, I think eventually it’ll probably become more female as well. I think it’ll always be male (yeah) but there might be more women.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. OK that’s everything you’ve been very helpful.
